title: Playwright: what it is, who builds it, what it drives
summary: Playwright is a browser automation library built and maintained by Microsoft. One API drives three browser engines (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) on Windows, macOS and Linux, headless or headed. It ships bindings for TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Java and .NET.

title: Its main job is end-to-end testing, with a built-in test runner
summary: Playwright ships @playwright/test, a full test runner with auto-waiting, web-first assertions, parallel workers, retries and HTML reports. This is the primary, most-documented use: writing a script that opens a real page, clicks and types like a user, and asserts what should be on screen.

title: It also runs with no test runner at all, as a plain scripting library
summary: The docs describe a separate "library" mode: import playwright, launch a browser, drive a page — no test framework involved. This is the mode behind web scraping, PDF generation and one-off automation scripts; the same API, used for tasks instead of assertions.

title: Screenshots and visual-regression testing are a core feature
summary: page.screenshot() captures full pages or elements as PNG/JPEG; Playwright Test adds toHaveScreenshot(), which compares a new screenshot pixel-by-pixel against a saved baseline and fails the test on a visible difference. This is the standard way teams catch unintended CSS/layout changes automatically.

title: page.pdf() renders any page to a real PDF file
summary: Playwright can generate a PDF of a loaded page using print CSS by default, or screen styling if you call emulateMedia() first. Used for invoices, reports and "export this page as PDF" features. Chromium only, and only in Playwrights own headless Chromium (not arbitrary headless Chrome builds).

title: Synthetic monitoring: run a Playwright script on a schedule to watch a live site
summary: A whole category of tools (Checkly, OneUptime and others) run a Playwright script every few minutes from outside your infrastructure to check that a real user flow (login, checkout, search) still works, alerting before a person notices. Same API as testing, aimed at production instead of CI.

title: Accessibility audits: Playwright itself has no checker, but plugs into axe-core
summary: Playwrights own docs say it has no built-in accessibility test; instead you install @axe-core/playwright, which runs the industry-standard axe engine against the live page and flags missing/invalid ARIA properties, poor color contrast and duplicate IDs. The docs are explicit that automated checks only catch some problems — manual review is still required.

title: Form automation: fill, check, select and upload, all with real actions
summary: Playwright provides locator.fill() for text fields, setChecked() for checkboxes/radios, selectOption() for dropdowns and setInputFiles() for file uploads, plus real click/type/keyboard events. It fills out and submits forms the way a person would, not by editing values through JavaScript.

title: The standard automation setup: run on every push, in GitHub Actions
summary: Playwrights own CI guide gives a ready-made GitHub Actions workflow: clone, install Node, install Playwright browsers, run tests, upload the HTML report as an artifact, triggered on every push and pull request to main. This is the default way teams wire it into a pipeline, not a special integration.

title: Codegen: record clicks in a real browser, get working test code back
summary: npx playwright codegen opens a real browser plus a recorder panel; every click, type and navigation you do by hand is turned into Playwright script as you go, including picking a good selector. The usual pattern is to record a rough script this way, then hand-clean it.

title: Trace Viewer: time-travel debugging for a failed run, no re-run needed
summary: With --trace on, Playwright records a DOM snapshot, screenshot, console log and every network request for each step of a run into one zip file. trace.playwright.dev opens that zip in the browser (nothing uploaded) and lets you scrub through the whole test like a video, which is how most flaky-CI failures actually get diagnosed.

title: Auto-waiting: Playwright checks five conditions before every action, automatically
summary: Before a click, Playwright waits for the element to be visible, stable (not still animating), able to receive the click (nothing covering it), enabled and, for a click specifically, not obscured — no manual sleep() calls. This single feature is what most comparisons point to as Playwrights biggest advantage over older tools.

title: Device emulation: one API for viewport, mobile, geolocation, locale and dark mode
summary: A single context can emulate a named device (viewport, user agent, touch), override locale and timezone, grant geolocation/notification permissions, and force a light or dark color scheme, all without touching real devices. Common use: proving a responsive layout actually works on a phone-sized viewport before shipping.

title: Network mocking: intercept, fake or block any request the page makes
summary: page.route() lets a script intercept a request before it hits the network and fulfill() it with a fake response, or abort() it entirely (useful for blocking images/ads to speed up a run, or testing an error state the real backend cannot easily produce on demand).

title: Headless browsers carry detectable fingerprints, and anti-bot services read them
summary: A default headless Chromium sets navigator.webdriver to true and lacks normal plugins/WebGL signatures; commercial anti-bot systems (Cloudflare, DataDome, Akamai) check exactly these markers and block or CAPTCHA-gate the request. This is a real, documented arms race, not a rumor — an entire "stealth plugin" ecosystem exists solely to patch these tells.

title: CAPTCHA-bypass automation: common practice to some, abuse-circumvention to others
summary: A real commercial ecosystem (CAPSolver, ZenRows, Bright Data and others) sells services to auto-solve reCAPTCHA and Cloudflare Turnstile from inside Playwright scripts. Whether this is normal scraping tooling or deliberate circumvention of a sites anti-abuse controls is genuinely disputed — it is legal gray area in most jurisdictions and against most sites own terms.

title: Auto-waiting cuts a lot of flakiness, but does not remove the cause
summary: Playwrights docs frame auto-waiting as solving timing flakiness. Practitioner postmortems disagree with the emphasis: they trace ongoing flakiness in real suites to async data arriving after an element looks "ready," CSS animations mid-transition, and locators matching the wrong element — causes auto-waiting cannot see, because it only checks the DOM, not application state.

title: Web scraping legality: public data is not a CFAA crime, but it can still be a broken contract
summary: In hiQ v. LinkedIn, the 9th Circuit ruled scraping publicly visible pages does not violate the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, even after a cease-and-desist. But hiQ still lost overall: the parties later settled with a $500,000 judgment against hiQ under California trespass-to-chattels and misappropriation law. "Not a CFAA crime" and "legally safe" are not the same claim.

title: The official Playwright MCP server: an accessibility snapshot, not a screenshot
summary: Microsofts @playwright/mcp gives an agent tools like navigate, click, type and snapshot; by default it hands back a structured accessibility-tree snapshot (roles, names, text) instead of a picture. This is a deliberate design choice, stated in the README: no vision model needed, and element targeting is exact instead of guessed from pixels.

title: How an agent drives a browser through MCP: snapshot, act, snapshot again
summary: The working loop is: ask for a snapshot of the page, choose an action against a specific element named in that snapshot (click ref=e14), then snapshot again to see what changed and decide the next step. This repeats until the task is done — closer to reading a form and filling it in than to looking at a photo.

title: A second, different approach exists: Anthropics computer use is pixel-and-coordinate driven
summary: Computer use gives Claude a screenshot plus mouse/keyboard tools (left_click at an x,y coordinate, type, scroll) — it reasons over an image, not a DOM tree. Anthropics own docs warn it still sometimes assumes an outcome without checking, and struggles with dropdowns and small text — the opposite trade-off from MCPs accessibility-tree approach.

title: Claude for Chrome: the same browser-control ability, wired into the tab you are already using
summary: Anthropics Chrome extension lets Claude click, type and read a live tab through a side panel, expanding from a 1,000-user pilot (Aug 2025) to all paid plans by Dec 2025. Anthropics own red-team numbers: prompt-injection attacks succeeded 23.6% of the time before mitigations, 11.2% after; browser-specific attacks fell from 35.7% to 0% with new safeguards. Anthropic says work remains before general availability.

title: Practitioner reports on Claude/Playwright test generation: real productivity, real new failure mode
summary: Vendor write-ups report Claude Code can generate working Playwright tests from a plain-English description, and that giving it project context (a CLAUDE.md, JSDoc) makes the output match a teams real style instead of generic scripts. The same sources flag a genuine new risk: an agentic "healer" that silently patches a broken test can hide a real product bug instead of surfacing it.

title: Accessibility-tree agents may age better than pixel-clicking agents for routine web tasks
summary: The case for MCP-style snapshot automation over computer-use-style pixel clicking: a DOM node keeps a stable identity across a resize or a font change, a screen coordinate does not. Nobody has published a head-to-head reliability study; this is an argument from how each system works, not a measured result — worth watching, not yet a settled fact.

title: This repo already runs Playwright headless for UI proof: the ui-test skill
summary: The ui-test skill drives real pointer gestures (drag, resize, sort) against this sites own pages with a plain Playwright script, and writes a screenshot plus a measured rect after every single step — the evidence is the numbers, not a description. Proven on ext/grip (a drawer resized 304 to 448px, exactly matching a +150 drag) and ext/Draggable (a real reorder, ghost element alive mid-drag).

title: This repo also runs Playwright to feed screenshots to a vision model, for design critique
summary: ext/DesignTool/vision shoots a page at set widths with headless Playwright, then sends the PNG to Claude with a fixed prompt and logs one JSONL line per shot. Measured cost: about $0.07 a shot on Sonnet. Its own findings warn that asking the model to grade a design (0-100) barely beats chance, but asking for a plain-English "direction" (nudge it left, make it bigger) was right 28 of 30 times.

title: Tonight this repo is building /websites/tools/: Playwright scripts to capture and tag real sites
summary: The parallel overnight brief plans Node-only Playwright tools that load a real external site once per width (400/1280/1920/3440, plus a 1280x4000 "long" shot), save it as jpeg, and pull its CSS from network responses (not the CSSOM, which throws cross-origin) — feeding a corpus of tagged layouts. Not yet built at the time of writing; this is the plan, not a result.

title: Playwright vs Puppeteer: same maker-lineage, Puppeteer stays Chrome-only
summary: Puppeteer (Google) drives Chrome/Edge and, more recently, Firefox, in JavaScript only, and is a library rather than a full test framework — no built-in assertions or parallel runner. Playwright (built by ex-Puppeteer engineers at Microsoft) adds Firefox and WebKit, four languages, and a complete test runner on top. For a Chrome-only scraping script the two are close; for cross-browser testing Playwright is the more complete tool.

title: Playwright vs Selenium: Selenium wins on breadth, Playwright on built-in reliability
summary: Selenium implements the W3C WebDriver standard, supported across Java, Python, C#, Ruby, PHP and JavaScript, and is the only one of the four with that language breadth and a decade-plus of enterprise tooling behind it. Playwright talks to browsers more directly and bundles auto-waiting, network interception and browser-context isolation as first-class features Selenium leaves to add-on libraries.

title: Playwright vs Cypress: Cypress runs inside the browser, and says so as a permanent trade-off
summary: Cypresss own docs list this as a permanent (not "coming soon") limitation: JavaScript/TypeScript only, one browser tab at a time, and one origin per test (cy.origin works around cross-origin navigation, but multi-tab needs a separate Puppeteer plugin). Playwright supports multiple tabs, multiple origins and four languages natively. Cypresss trade-off buys a distinctive in-browser debugging experience in return.

title: A widely repeated "42% faster, 67% fewer flaky tests" stat has no traceable source
summary: Several 2026 comparison articles cite "Playwright is 42% faster than Selenium and produces 67% fewer flaky tests than Cypress, across 300+ suites analyzed by TestDino" as if it were settled data. No underlying study, methodology or raw numbers were locatable — the figure appears to originate from one vendors own content and gets repeated by others without a citation. Treat specific numbers like this as marketing until a primary source turns up.

title: What would actually settle "which of these four is best"?
summary: Every comparison above is a real trade-off (language count vs auto-waiting vs in-browser DX vs raw speed), not a ranking — nobody has published a controlled study running the same real test suite on all four tools under the same conditions. Without one, "Playwright is faster/more reliable" stays an aggregate impression from many small, self-selected reports, not a measured fact.
